newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Court limits application of national rules on trademark.
newsitem.headline: Court limits application of national rules on trademark.

text.p: The European Court of Justice said on Thursday member states may not use national trademark rules as a pretense to limit intra-EU trade.
The owner of a trademark protected by legislation of one member state may not restrict parallel imports where the manufacturer has permitted the sale of a product in another member state.

The court said it made no difference whether the product had been manufactured in a non-member country if it had been lawfully entered into the EU market by the owner of the mark or with the owner's consent, including marketing by another company in the same group as the owner.
"Articles 30 and 36 of the EC Treaty - Trade Mark Directive - Plant health product - Parallel import - Exhaustion"
Reference from the Tribunal de Commerce, Pontoise, France, for a preliminary ruling in the proceedings between
on the interpretation of articles 30 and 36 of the EC treaty

Article 7 of the First Council directive 89/104/EEC of 21 December 1988 to approximate the laws of the member states relating to trade marks is to be interpreted as precluding application of a national rule in member state A under which the owner of a trade mark may prevent importation of a product protected by the mark where
-- the product has been manufactured in a non-member country,
-- it has been imported into member state B by the owner of the mark or by another company in the same group as the owner of the mark
-- it has been lawfully acquired in member state B by an independent trader, who has exported it to member state A

-- it has not been processed and the packaging has not been changed, apart from the addition to the label of certain information to comply with the requirements of the legislation of the member state of import, and
-- the trade mark rights are held in member states A and B by the same group.
